blocks.x: Later this month, J. Press will open a new flagship store at the corner of Madison Avenue and East 44th Street in Manhattan. The store, with its wood panels, old photographs, and letters to the company penned by former American presidents, feels suitably reverent for a clothier on the eve of its 125th anniversary, and a natural complement to the stacks of rugby shirts, tweed sport coats, and other Ivy League staples within. It’s also a homecoming of sorts for J. Press, which operated a store across the street from 1932 to 2014. Students of American menswear will note that the intersection is the longtime home of the Brooks Brothers building, which was built in 1915 as the flagship of J. Press’s more famous Ivy League rival and has sat empty since the brand filed for bankruptcy in 2020.

This significance is not lost on J. Press creative director and president Jack Carlson, who was finalizing a deal to take over the former Brooks Brothers space when the building was sold. The founder of Rowing Blazers, a prep revival label specializing in colorful takes on Ivy staples, Carlson is now tasked with leading J. Press through the biggest expansion in the brand’s history. Over the next four years, J. Press intends to expand its footprint in the United States, opening as many as 20 new stores in an effort to increase its sales tenfold to $100 million per year. It’s an ambitious plan, and as the crumbling hulk of the Brooks Brothers building attests, growth on that scale is both complicated and risky. The fashion business is notoriously fickle, especially for mid-market brands like J. Press, and the road to success is littered with the corpses of promising labels that succumbed to changing tastes, economic downturns, and the demands of private equity.

To reach his goal, Carlson will need to attract a host of new fashion-oriented customers while appealing to a base of old-school menswear aficionados who bristle at the idea of J. Press as a capital-F fashion brand, particularly given the fashion industry’s reputation for low-quality, high-volume churn. Still, Carlson is bullish on his prospects. “I’m not trying to be flippant about it, but $100 million is not a massive company. That’s where we probably should be, if J. Press and Ivy style matter in the conversation,” he says. “From my perspective, a lot of what we need to do to grow is doubling down on the things that make J. Press J. Press.”

Press earned a reputation as a chief purveyor of Ivy League style, a form of dress that blended traditional English tailoring with the American sportswear favored by the sons of the Northeastern elite. Name-checked by F. Scott Fitzgerald and Tom Wolfe, and worn by a who’s who of 20th century style icons including Cary Grant, Miles Davis, and John F. Kennedy, J. Press has done as much to define modern American menswear as any other brand. Among its signature offerings are Oxford-collar button-down shirts (a.k.a. OCBDs), soft-shouldered navy blazers with gold buttons, and—perhaps most famously—the Shaggy Dog sweater, a Scottish wool crewneck named for its fluffy, brushed surface.

J. Press was family-owned until 1986, when it was sold—with the blessing of the Press family—to Japanese clothing group Onward Holdings, which had been licensed to sell J. Press in Japan since the 1970s. Over the next four decades, Onward expanded the brand throughout its home country, where Ivy style, like all things Americana, has been popular since the 1960s, and it now operates 80 J. Press stores in Japan.

On the other side of the world, Carlson’s strategy of doubling down on J. Press’s core identity had its first test in February when he presented the brand’s first-ever fashion show at New York Fashion Week. The show’s theme was Take Ivy, a canonical menswear book that documented the wardrobes of Ivy League students—many of whom wore J. Press—in the 1960s. For the show and accompanying campaign, Carlson blended recreations of specific looks from the book with modern, fashion-oriented pieces like collegiate sweatshirts with “TAKE IVY” emblazoned across the chest. The halo piece was a $1,500 blaze orange waxed cotton raincoat made to order by New York-based designer Léo Guarin in a limited edition of five.

blocks.x: The collection drew mixed reviews, but the hottest take came from rapper, designer, and noted prep revivalist Tyler, The Creator. “damn yall didnt wanna change a color or nothing to make it yalls own or make it something a little different,” he wrote on Instagram, in his signature lowercase style, about the coat. Tyler later walked back his comments, and Carlson made a peace offering of a limited-edition raincoat, but his sentiments captured the essential conundrum facing a 125-year-old brand trying to reinvent itself in 2026: rehash the past, and people will say you’re phoning it in; stray too far from it, and you’ll be accused of taking the brand in the wrong direction.

“You’re always going to have the real fashion guy who was hoping for something way more avant‑garde, and you’re always going to have the self‑anointed reactionary guy whose personal definition of Ivy is the be‑all and end‑all,” Carlson says. “If you spent your whole time worrying about what this person or that person might say, you'd never really get anywhere. I'm not going to be too hung up on what Tyler or anybody else might say, but I’ll certainly invite Tyler to the show, and I hope he comes.”

Despite some online criticism, longtime fans of the brand seem willing to let Carlson cook. “Generally, I think J. Press is headed in the right direction,” says Will Eaton, the moderator of r/NavyBlazer, a Reddit community devoted to Ivy style in which J. Press is a frequent topic of conversation. “Although Jack Carlson has launched a few gimmicky collaborations, I’m pretty happy with his overall direction. For example, he’s discussed revamping their Oxford shirts to get a better collar roll. That’s a minor detail for most people, but also one of the most distinctive features of a shirt for those in the know.” While Eaton is concerned about how the brand’s expansion might impact the quality of its wares, he’s pleased to see things like high-end fabrics from Fox Brothers, a centuries-old British mill, and a renewed focus on products made in the United States and Europe.

Press has an incredible legacy, but through the 20th century, the clientele became older and limited to trad purists,” he says. “J. Press was fundamental to the creation of the original Ivy League style, and I’m excited to see it play a role in defining the much broader and more inclusive idea of Ivy League style for this century.”

The fall-winter 2026 collection, which was built around classic British textiles like tweed, Fox Brothers flannel, Barbour waxed cotton, and Fair Isle knits, is a nod to Ivy style’s origins as sporting clothes worn by the British aristocracy. It’s also, thanks to some cheeky iconography and pops of blaze orange, cobalt blue, and camo, unmistakably modern.

A cast diverse in age and ethnicity walked the runway, subtly reflecting the brand’s aspirations to transform what was once the exclusive territory of wealthy East Coast WASPs into something that can be worn by anyone. It also spoke to Jacobi Press’s status as an outsider to that world. “Jacobi Press came to America from Latvia and he didn’t grow up with any of this British stuff. But he had a keen eye, impeccable taste, and uncompromising standards,” Carlson writes. “He was kind of the Ralph Lauren of his day—he created an idealized version of the world he imagined at Cambridge and Oxford, and on great British country estates.”

blocks.x: The star of the J. Press fall-winter collection is the Shaggy Dog sweater, now available in more than 75 styles and colors ranging from crewnecks to polos. Carlson believes the Shaggy Dog embodies everything the new J. Press can be: versatile enough to appeal to a wide range of customers, but still made with the same attention to quality and authentic Ivy style as it was in the brand’s heyday. “The Shaggy Dog is a very important thing in the canon of J. Press,” he says. “A lot of brands have something they call a Shetland sweater, but J. Press is, I think, the only American brand where the Shetland sweaters are made in Shetland, using Shetland wool.”

While creating the new collection, Carlson traveled to the Shetland Islands, a remote archipelago in northern Scotland, where sheep outnumber people ten to one. He describes how each Shaggy Dog is hand-brushed by a single craftsman (his name is Ian, and his grandfather did the job before him) with a traditional tool called a teasel, made from the head of a local flower. Scaling production of Shaggy Dog sweaters for the fall season has been challenging, he admits, and the factory has been running around the clock to meet the deadline. Instead of moving production elsewhere, though, he plans to make the factory part of J. Press’s long-term plan. “The answer is not like, ‘Okay, you know what, we're going to have to move to China.’ It’s growing the factory and growing the capacity right there in Shetland,” Carlson says. “Ian’s going to have to have a friend sitting next to him with more teasels, and then eventually they might have to have a room of people brushing with teasels that Ian can supervise.”

It’s a beautiful idea, but whether this vision of J.Press’s future—in which customers, suppliers, and corporate bosses all get what they want—will actually come to pass remains to be seen. For now, the brand has some good things going for it, including a revered name, a (mostly) enthusiastic customer base, and a creative director who’s passionate about Ivy style and appears genuinely committed to doing things the right way. “We’re not just pumping out clothes,” says Carlson. “There is almost a higher purpose that we're pursuing, and that makes it worthwhile in and of itself. J. Press is in some ways the last remaining standard-bearer for classic American menswear, and a lot of my job is not fucking it up.”
